sections.body:
Every workplace has a second language under the first one. It is made of phrases that are used so often that nobody explains them, and they are rarely literal. "Let us circle back to that" does not mean returning to a circle. "That is a great idea" does not always mean the idea is good.

These expressions exist because offices are places where people have to be careful with each other. Nobody wants to say "I disagree with you" at 09:00 on a Monday, so they say "I see it slightly differently". Nobody wants to say "you made a mistake", so they say "there is a small gap in the numbers". The phrases are not decoration. They are the mechanism by which people criticise, refuse, delay and disagree without creating a conflict.

That is why learning them matters more than learning vocabulary. Words are easy to look up. The difficulty is knowing what "let's park that for now" really means in an office, and what it implies about who has the power to decide.

There are six families of workplace expression, and this article goes through each one. **Meetings**: how to talk about time, agenda and outcome. **Deadlines and pressure**: how to say a thing is late, urgent or blocked. **Money and career**: how people talk about pay, budgets and promotion. **People**: how colleagues, managers and clients are described. **Problems**: how mistakes, risks and fixes are named. **Decisions**: how agreement and disagreement are made to sound.

Two rules make the whole subject easier. First, **an expression is a piece of social meaning, not a word**. It tells you what the speaker wants you to do, and it says something about the relationship between you. Second, **the meaning depends on the tone**. "We need to talk" said warmly at 17:00 on a Friday is a meeting request; said coldly at 09:00 on a Monday it is a warning.

Read this and you will not only understand the phrases. You will know when to use them, when to use a plainer word instead, and how to explain one to a colleague who has never heard it.
examples: Let us circle back to the budget question after lunch.
There is a small gap in the numbers here, so let us check the source file.
We should park that for now and come back to it next week.
sections.heading: What a workplace expression is

sections.body:
Meetings generate more office language than anything else, because meetings are where the language does its work.

Let us circle back to that means we will return to the topic later. It is often a polite way of postponing something indefinitely. If you need a decision, say so: "Can we circle back to this by Friday, so it is not still open?"

Let us take this offline means the discussion should continue in a smaller group, usually two people, away from the meeting. It can also mean "stop talking about this", and it is often used when a topic is uncomfortable in front of the whole team.

Let us park that means to set a topic aside, on purpose, to deal with later. It is useful and honest. It is also a soft way of killing a topic without saying so.

Let us touch base means to have a short conversation. It comes from baseball, where a base is a point you return to. "Let us touch base on Thursday" is a request for fifteen minutes. **To loop someone in** means to bring a person into a conversation or a task, so they know about it: "I looped in Finance, since they will need to approve it."

A deep dive means a long, detailed look at one topic: "We did a deep dive on the churn numbers." **To run something by someone** means to ask for their opinion before you commit: "Can I run this by you before I send it?" **To walk someone through** something means to explain it step by step, as in a demonstration.

To wrap up means to finish a discussion and summarise it. **To wrap something up** can also mean to finish a piece of work, and it carries an unpleasant undertone when the work is bad: "We need to wrap this project up; nobody is using it."

To get something off the ground means to start it and make it happen. **To take something from idea to reality** means the same thing, more grandly. **To keep something on track** means to stop it from slipping, which is a normal job description for a project manager.

The one expression worth knowing in detail is **the ball is in your court**. It means the next move is yours: I have done my part, now it is your turn. It is neutral in tone but firm: "The report is with the legal team, so the ball is in their court."
examples: Let us take this offline after the meeting and I will send you the numbers.
Let us touch base on Thursday for fifteen minutes.
I looped in Finance, since they will need to approve the payment.
The contract is signed, so the ball is in our court now.
Can I run this by you before I send it to the client?
sections.heading: Expressions about meetings and time

sections.body:
Work is mostly about time, and so a large part of office language is about time.

To run late means to be behind schedule. **To be on track** means to be going as planned. **To be ahead of schedule** is the good version. **To slip** means a date moves later: "The launch date has slipped by two weeks." Note that the date slips, not the person; this is a common way to describe a delay without blaming anyone.

To push something back means to move a date to a later one. **To push back on something** also means to object to it, which is a different meaning in the same family: "The client pushed back on the price." Note the double meaning and pick the one that fits your sentence.

To flag something means to raise it as an issue, usually early: "I want to flag a risk in the schedule." **To raise** something is the plainer version. **To escalate** means to take something to a more senior person, and it should be used only when a normal route has failed.

To be stretched means to have too much work: "We are stretched thin this month." **To be swamped** is the same thing, more casual. **To juggle** means to manage several things at once: "I am juggling two projects and the audit." **To be at capacity** means you cannot take more work, in a formal register.

To get someone up to speed means to bring them to a level of understanding where they can help: "Let me get you up to speed on the supplier issue." **To onboard** someone means to bring a new person into a team or a company, and it is now a job title: "She is onboarding two new engineers."

To hit a snag means to meet a difficulty that stops progress for a moment: "We hit a snag with the import licence." A **snag** is small; a **blocker** or a **showstopper** is not. **To be blocked** means you cannot continue until someone else does something.

To get the ball rolling and **to get something off the ground** mean to start something. **To turn things around** means to improve a situation quickly: "The new team turned the account around in a quarter." **To keep things moving** means to avoid a standstill.

One warning. **To bite the bullet** means to do something unpleasant that you have been avoiding. It comes from old surgery and it is vivid. In a formal email to a new client, choose plainer words.
examples: The launch date has slipped by two weeks, but the scope has not changed.
I want to flag a risk in the schedule before it becomes a problem.
Let me get you up to speed on the supplier issue.
We hit a snag with the import licence, so we are waiting on the customs office.
We are stretched thin this month, so I can only take one new item.
sections.heading: Expressions about deadlines, delays and pressure

sections.body:
Money is the topic of the workplace where plain words are hardest, and expressions do a lot of the politeness work.

A pay rise and **a raise** are the same thing. **A salary review** is a formal discussion of your pay, usually with a manager, often annual. **To benchmark** means to compare your pay or your offer with what the market pays. **A benchmark figure** is that comparison number.

Ballpark means an approximate figure, and it is informal: "Can you give me a ballpark figure for the full build?" **An estimate** is a number with some accuracy; a **quote** or **quotation** is a formal offer of price; an **invoice** is a request for payment after the work is done.

To budget for something means to plan and set aside money for it. **To blow the budget** means to go over it. **To cut costs** means to reduce spending. **To freeze budgets** means to stop any changes until further notice, which is a sign of trouble in a company.

To get a promotion is to move up a level. **To move up** is the same. **To be promoted** is the passive form, and it is what a company says about you: "She was promoted to team lead in March." **To take on more responsibility** is a soft, common way to ask for more work, and often more pay.

To put someone forward for promotion means to recommend them. **To put a case forward** means to argue for something, usually with reasons. **To have a case** means to have enough evidence to argue: "I do not have a strong case for an exception this time."

To make the case means to argue that something is worth doing, usually with numbers. **To get buy-in** means to get other people to agree and support something: "I spent two weeks getting buy-in from the regional teams." **To sign off** means to give formal approval, and **sign-off** is the approval itself. **To get sign-off from Finance** is a normal step in a process.

Two expressions with sharp edges. **To gold-plate** means to add features nobody asked for, usually to look impressive: "We did not gold-plate it; we shipped what was needed." **To throw good money after bad** means to spend more on something that has already failed, in the hope of saving it.
examples: Could you give me a ballpark figure for the full build?
I would like to book a salary review for the end of the quarter.
I spent two weeks getting buy-in from the regional teams.
We do not have a strong case for an exception this time.
We are looking at moving you up to team lead in the next cycle.
sections.heading: Expressions about money, budgets and promotion

sections.body:
How colleagues are described tells you a great deal about the culture of a company.

A stakeholder is anyone affected by a decision: staff, customers, suppliers, regulators. **To keep stakeholders informed** is a standard duty. **To manage up** means to work well with your manager, especially to give them what they need; it is never an insult. **To manage down** means to lead your team well.

To onboard someone is to bring them into the team. **To mentor** is to guide someone in their development. **To shadow** someone is to watch them work in order to learn. **To buddy up** with someone means to pair up, usually a newcomer with an experienced colleague. **To hand over** means to pass work and responsibility to someone else, and **a handover** is that transfer, often written down.

To get along with someone means to have a good relationship. **To have a good working relationship with** is the professional version of the same thing, and it appears in almost every job description. **To rub someone up the wrong way** means to annoy them, and it is a strong phrase; do not use it about a senior person. **To get on someone’s nerves** is the milder version.

A point of contact is the person to go to about something. **To be the point of contact** is a small but visible responsibility. **To be the go-to person** for something means you are the one everyone asks. **To be in the loop** means to be informed and up to date; **to loop someone in** means to inform them; **to be out of the loop** means to have missed what is happening.

To get cold feet means to lose your nerve and change your mind before an action: "They got cold feet about the relocation offer." **To have a change of heart** is the same thing, gentler. **To walk away from** something means to leave it, usually a project, a deal or a negotiation.

And one very common expression: **to wear many hats**. It means to do several different jobs, often in a small team: "In a company this size, everyone wears many hats." It is normally said with pride rather than complaint, and it is a good phrase to use when you want to explain why you have been busy.
examples: I will be the point of contact for the supplier from now on.
Please keep the regional managers in the loop on the change.
We are a small team, so everyone wears many hats.
She was the go-to person for anything to do with customs paperwork.
They got cold feet about the relocation offer and withdrew.
sections.heading: Expressions about people and relationships

sections.body:
How a workplace talks about failure tells you whether people are safe there.

A mistake is an error by someone. **An error** is the same, more formal. **To own the mistake** means to admit it publicly and take responsibility, and it is a compliment: "I want to own the mistake and explain what we will do differently." **To point the finger** means to blame someone else, and it is strongly negative.

To learn from our mistakes sounds positive but is often said after something has gone badly. **To move forward** means to stop looking back at it. **To put it behind us** means the same, and it can be genuine or a way of dodging a real issue.

A quick fix solves the problem for now, and the standard warning follows: **a quick fix is not a long-term solution**. **A band-aid** is a temporary fix; the plural **band-aids** is used for a lot of temporary fixes: "We have applied three band-aids to this process and it still fails." **A workaround** is a way of working around a problem without solving it. **To iron out** problems means to remove small ones: "We ironed out the details in the contract."

To get to the bottom of something means to find the real cause: "We need to get to the bottom of the repeated delays." **To troubleshoot** means to search for the cause. **To address** an issue means to deal with it, and it is the safest professional verb there is: "I will address the issue before Friday."

To put out fires means to deal with urgent problems all day instead of doing planned work: "I have been putting out fires all week." **A fire drill** is a practice run, and a **drill** in general is a rehearsal. **To be on fire** means to be extremely busy, and it is American slang but widely understood.

Low-hanging fruit means the easy wins: "We picked the low-hanging fruit first and delivered in three weeks." It is a metaphor, and it means quick results rather than difficult ones. **A quick win** means the same thing in plainer words.

And one that sounds generous but is not always: **to throw good money after bad**. If you keep spending on a project that has already failed, that is what you are doing.
examples: I want to own the mistake and explain what we will do differently.
We applied three band-aids to this process and it still fails.
We need to get to the bottom of the repeated delays.
I have been putting out fires all week and have not touched the audit.
We picked the low-hanging fruit first and delivered in three weeks.
sections.heading: Expressions about problems, mistakes and fixes

sections.body:
This is where the indirectness of office English is strongest, and where misreading a phrase costs you most.

To be on the same page means to agree, or to have the same understanding: "Let us make sure we are on the same page about the deadline." It is very common and always safe.

To agree on something is to settle it. **To sign off on something** is to approve it formally. **To green-light** something is to give permission for it to start: "Legal has green-lighted the launch." **A green light** is the permission itself. The opposite is **to red-flag** something, which means to mark it as a warning: "The report red-flags the risk to the schedule."

To have buy-in is to have support. **To be a hard sell** means something is difficult to persuade people about: "A four-day week is a hard sell in this department." **To sell someone on something** means to persuade them: "I need to sell her on the new plan."

To push back means to object. **To raise concerns** is the polite, standard way to object in writing. **To have reservations** is to have doubts without stating them outright. **To have doubts** is the same, plainer. **To be sceptical** is to doubt openly, and it is stronger than sceptical-sounding phrasing.

The phrase that causes the most confusion is **that is a great idea**, said with a flat tone. In many offices it means the opposite, and it is often a politeness wrapper around a no. If you suspect this, do not accept it. Say: "Are we agreed on that, then?" and get a straight answer. **To buy time** means to delay a decision while you think, or while you look for a way out of it.

Two more. **To table a discussion** means to put it on the agenda for a meeting, or, in British English, to postpone it; the meaning depends on the office. **To go back to the drawing board** means to start the work again from the beginning because the first approach failed: "We are going back to the drawing board on the design."
examples: Let us make sure we are on the same page about the deadline.
Legal has green-lighted the launch for June.
The report red-flags the risk to the schedule.
Are we agreed on that, then?
We are going back to the drawing board on the design.
sections.heading: Expressions about decisions, agreement and disagreement

sections.body:
How a workplace talks about effort is where the culture shows itself most clearly.

To go the extra mile means to do more than the job requires: "She always goes the extra mile for the customer." **To go above and beyond** is the same, stronger. **To go the extra mile** can also be used critically, meaning someone works too much without being paid for it, and that reading is becoming more common.

To pull your weight means to do your fair share of the work, and the opposite is **to free-ride**: to benefit from a group without contributing. **To carry the team** means to do the work that holds everyone else up. **To pick up the slack** means to take on work that nobody else did.

To raise the bar means to improve the standard; **to set the bar** means to define it; **to lower the bar** is negative. **To raise expectations** is about what people are promised, not about quality.

To be on top of things means to be well organised. **To have a handle on something** means to control or understand it: "I do not have a handle on the schedule yet." **To get on top of** means to bring it under control. **To keep on top of** means to keep it there.

For pressure: **to be under the weather** means to feel slightly unwell, and it is not used to mean tired. **To be burnt out** or **to burn out** means exhaustion from sustained work, and it is serious. **To be on a high** at work means to be very busy, usually with a deadline. **To be slammed** is American but widely understood. **To be in the weeds** means to be deep in the detail, often uncomfortably so: "We got into the weeds on the data model."

And **to be on the same page** has a cousin: **to be on the back foot**, which means to be defending yourself in a situation where you are being pushed, usually by bad news: "We have been on the back foot since the supplier changed the terms."
examples: She always goes the extra mile for the customer.
I do not have a handle on the schedule yet.
We got into the weeds on the data model, so let us step back.
We have been on the back foot since the supplier changed the terms.
Everyone has to pick up the slack before Friday.
sections.heading: Expressions about effort, performance and stress

sections.body:
Office expressions are usually slang versions of ordinary words. Knowing the plain version keeps you out of trouble.

Band-aid means a temporary fix. **Workaround** means a way of avoiding the problem rather than solving it. **Band-aid and workaround** are not the same as a **solution**.

Circle back means to return to a topic later. **Follow up** means the same, and it is plainer. **Touch base** means to have a short conversation. **Check in** means the same thing.

Take offline means to move a discussion out of the meeting. **Take aside** means the same. **Park** means to set aside for later. **Postpone** is the plain version of both.

Flag means to raise an issue. **Raise** is the plainer word. **Escalate** means to take something to a more senior level. **Escalate to management** is the common phrase.

Green-light means to approve. **Approve** is the plain version. **Sign off** means to give formal approval. **Buy-in** means support or agreement. **Buy-in from the team** is the usual phrase.

Headwind is an obstacle working against you, usually from outside: **a headwind from the new regulations**. **Tailwind** is a helpful force: **the tailwind of a strong market**. **Headwind** has become common in business English worldwide.

Low-hanging fruit means the easy wins. **Quick win** is the plain version. **Low-effort** means needing little work, and it is slightly dismissive.

Ramp up means to increase activity, output or skill: **ramping up production**. **Ramp up** can also mean to train someone: **to ramp up a new joiner**.

Ballpark means an approximate figure. **Estimate** is the plain word. **Ballpark figure** is the usual phrase.

Deep dive means a long, detailed examination. **Detailed review** is the plain version. **Deep dive** is used a lot in business and is now understood almost everywhere.

Bandwidth is the capacity of a person or a team to take on work, and it now comes from computing. **I do not have the bandwidth this week** means I am too busy. The plain version is **I am too busy this week**, and the plain version is better in writing.
sections.heading: The plain words behind the expressions

terms.example: We applied a band-aid to the payment process, but the real fix is in the accounting system.
terms.gloss: A temporary fix that makes a problem go away without solving it.

terms.example: The manual workaround is for us to check the total by hand every Friday.
terms.gloss: A way of working around a problem instead of fixing its cause.

terms.example: Let us circle back to the budget question after lunch.
terms.gloss: To return to a topic later. Often used to postpone a decision.

terms.example: Can we touch base on Thursday for fifteen minutes?
terms.gloss: To have a short conversation with someone about something.

terms.example: Let us take this offline and I will send you the figures.
terms.gloss: To move a discussion out of the meeting into a smaller group.

terms.example: I want to flag a risk in the schedule before it becomes a problem.
terms.gloss: To raise an issue or a risk so that people notice it early.

terms.example: If we do not hear back by Friday, we will need to escalate this.
terms.gloss: To take a matter to a more senior person because it has not moved.

terms.example: Legal has green-lighted the launch for June.
terms.gloss: To give formal permission for something to go ahead.

terms.example: I still need sign-off from Finance before I send the order.
terms.gloss: Formal approval, and the act of giving it.

terms.example: I spent two weeks getting buy-in from the regional teams.
terms.gloss: Agreement and active support for a plan from the people who must carry it out.

terms.example: We are facing a headwind from the new import regulations.
terms.gloss: A force working against you, such as a rule change or a weak market.

terms.example: We picked the low-hanging fruit first and delivered in three weeks.
terms.gloss: The easy results, available with little effort before the harder work.

terms.example: We are ramping up production ahead of the festival season.
terms.gloss: To increase activity, output or capability, often over a planned period.

terms.example: We did a deep dive on the churn numbers before the review.
terms.gloss: A long, detailed examination of one subject.

terms.example: Could you give me a ballpark figure for the full build?
terms.gloss: A rough approximate number, given before the real figure is known.

terms.example: I do not have the bandwidth this week, but I can do it next month.
terms.gloss: The capacity a person or team has to take on more work.

sections.body:
The danger of learning workplace expressions is that you start using too many of them, and you sound like someone who has read a list.

One expression per message. In a short email, one idiom is plenty. Two or three in the same paragraph sounds forced and makes the reader work.

Use the plain version when the stakes are high. In writing to a client, in a message about a mistake, in an email to someone you do not know well, plainer words carry more weight. "The report was late because the supplier changed the specification" is better than "the supplier moved the goalposts, so we are behind".

Keep the subject matter ordinary. Idioms fit easily with everyday topics, because everyday topics are what they grew out of. "We need to circle back on the budget" is fine. "Let us touch base about the metaphorical journey of our shared enterprise" is not.

Pronounce them naturally. "Touch base" is said as two ordinary words. "Circle back" is two words. "Low-hanging fruit" has the stress on HANGING. If you are unsure, use a plainer phrase and nobody will mind.

Do not stack them. "Let us circle back and touch base to park the ball in your court" is three expressions doing one job.

Watch the level. Some of these phrases are quite informal among peers (**juggling**, **slammed**, **putting out fires**) and some are formal enough for a board (**stakeholders**, **escalation**, **sign-off**). Using a very informal expression with a senior person can read as careless; using a very formal one with a close colleague can read as distant.

And one habit that solves most of the problem. **Use the plain word when you are writing and the expression when you are speaking.** Email rewards clarity. Conversations reward speed, and in a fast conversation a plain sentence can sound slower than the shared shorthand. If you write "let us discuss this at the next meeting" but your colleague says "let us circle back", both are understood, and nobody is offended.
examples: Let us discuss this at the next meeting on Tuesday.
The report was late because the supplier changed the specification.
The supplier moved the goalposts, so the schedule slipped.
sections.heading: How to use these expressions without sounding fake

sections.body:
An idiom you half know. Half-understood idioms are worse than plain words, because they carry the tone without the meaning. If you are not sure what an expression means, do not use it.

An idiom that does not fit the culture. Some offices love informal language and some do not. Watch how people speak to you in the first two weeks, and match that.

An expression used sarcastically. "Great idea" said flatly means the opposite. "That is a great idea" repeated twice about the same plan means stop talking about it.

"That is a great idea" in writing. Never write this to mean "no". Write "I am not sure about that" or "We have a problem with that", or simply ask the question that gets a straight answer.

Too many at once. A paragraph of idioms is a wall. Use one, and let the rest of the sentence be ordinary.

The wrong idiom in the wrong place. "We need to talk" is a warning in many offices. If you mean a five-minute conversation, say "could we have a quick chat about the report".

Saying something you do not mean. "That is a great idea", "no worries", and "not a problem" are all ways of being polite. If you genuinely disagree, disagree. Being liked is less useful than being clear.
sections.heading: When an expression will backfire

item.summary: Every workplace has a layer of language that is not in the dictionary: phrases for a meeting, a delay, a mistake, a decision. After reading this you will understand the expressions you hear in offices, use them at the right moment, and avoid the ones that make you sound either too casual or too managerial.
item.title: Understanding Common Workplace Expressions
